changelog.change: Initial entry — MAC of the volatile agents (adult and > 60 y), MAC-awake / MAC-BAR, age adjustment, additivity, and the desflurane phase-out.

summary: 1 MAC = the alveolar concentration that prevents movement to a surgical incision in 50% of patients. MAC is additive (0.5 MAC sevoflurane + 0.5 MAC N₂O ≈ 1 MAC). It falls ~6% per decade of age and with opioids, benzodiazepines, alpha-2 agonists, hypothermia, hyponatraemia, pregnancy, and acute alcohol; it rises with chronic alcohol, stimulants, and hyperthermia.

Used at ~0.5–0.7 MAC to reduce the volatile requirement (second-gas effect, fast on/off). Avoid: pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, middle-ear / intra-ocular gas, pulmonary hypertension, first-trimester pregnancy, B12 deficiency

items: MAC-awake ≈ 0.3–0.4 MAC — the concentration at which 50% respond to command / open their eyes (roughly the threshold for recall on emergence).
MAC ≈ 1.0 — no movement to incision in 50%; aim for ~1.2–1.3 MAC (ED95) for surgical anaesthesia without opioid, less with opioid.
MAC-BAR ≈ 1.3–1.5 MAC — Blocks the Adrenergic Response (catecholamine surge) to incision in 50%.

body.text: MAC peaks in infancy (~6 months) and declines roughly 6% per decade thereafter. A practical estimate: MAC₄₀ × 10^(−0.00269 × (age − 40)) (Mapleson). Rule of thumb — at 80 y the volatile requirement is ~30% lower than at 40 y; titrate to a processed-EEG / clinical endpoint rather than a fixed dial, especially in the elderly.

Lowers MAC: increasing age, opioids, benzodiazepines, alpha-2 agonists (dexmedetomidine, clonidine), IV anaesthetics, lithium, acute alcohol / other CNS depressants, hypothermia, hyponatraemia, hypotension / anaemia (severe), pregnancy (~30% by term), and hypoxia / hypercapnia. Raises MAC: chronic alcohol use, chronic amphetamine / cocaine / MAOIs, acute cocaine, hyperthermia, hypernatraemia, and red hair (modestly). Duration of anaesthesia, sex, and PaCO₂ within the normal range do NOT change MAC.
